title: I have some bad news
author: Ian Hallett
summary: Hallett takes the familiar advice about not shooting the messenger and turns it into a measurable leadership diagnostic. He opens with Alan Mulally arriving at a Ford that was losing 12.7 billion dollars a year while every project chart in the weekly review came back green, then detours through the voice and silence research of Detert and Burris and of Milliken, Morrison and Hewlin to establish that people withhold bad news based on what they expect will happen to them. His central move is to reframe the delay between a problem starting and a leader hearing about it as a measurement of the leader rather than of the team. He then prescribes four actions in a fixed order, beginning with thanking the messenger in front of whoever is present and separating the review of what happened from any review of who did it. A section on failure modes names the fix-it reflex, the disbelieving question, the weather report and the instant answer that later gets reversed. The piece closes with a ten minute exercise: log the date somebody first knew against the date you found out for the next three problems, then ask the person who closed the shortest gap what made them decide to tell you when they did.
points: Hallett reframes the lag between a problem arising and a leader learning of it as a measurement of the leader, recalibrated by the team after every reaction.
He grounds the argument in two complementary studies of employee voice and employee silence rather than in anecdote alone.
The prescription is four sequenced actions, starting with visible thanks and ending with a strict separation of the what happened review from the who did it conversation.
He names four failure modes, including the fix-it reflex and the weather report, and notes that the weather report is invisible to the leader by definition.
The Mulally applause story is used carefully, with Hallett declining to credit Ford's survival to one round of clapping and crediting it instead with buying time.
quotes: Alan Mulally arrived at Ford in September 2006 and began running the same meeting every week. The same leaders, the same charts, and every project on them marked red, yellow or green.
The two studies describe the same thing from opposite ends. People withhold bad news because of what they expect will happen to them when they do.
So the gap between a problem starting and you hearing about it is a measurement of you. Your team takes that measurement every time, and they recalibrate it on whatever you did last.
Say you are glad they told you. Ask three questions before anything else. Buy time in one sentence if you do not have the facts. Review what happened before you review who did it.

Running the ‘what happened’ and ‘who did it’ discussions together means everyone present becomes their own defence counsel. You will get a defensible account instead of an accurate one, which is the only thing you need.
The weather report. Your team works out what mood you are in before deciding what to raise. This one you cannot see, because by the time anything reaches you it has already passed the test.
The question is not whether you raised your voice. It is what your face did in the two seconds before you spoke, and whether the next thing out of your mouth was a question or an instruction.
